subject: science
passage: Barnacle larvae drift in open water until they find a hard surface on which to settle for life, and ship hulls are a frequent target. In tests with painted panels hung from a dock, marine biologist Tomás Herrera found that larvae settled far more densely on dark panels than on light ones. Herrera attributes this preference to vision: dark surfaces, he proposes, resemble the shaded rock crevices where adult barnacles survive best. Another possibility, however, is that dark panels, which absorb more sunlight, grow a thicker film of bacteria, a film that may itself attract settling larvae.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Herrera's explanation?

choices.A: Larvae settled more densely on dark panels than on light ones even when all the panels were kept free of bacteria.
choices.B: Light panels coated with the bacterial film taken from dark panels attracted as many larvae as dark panels did.
choices.C: Barnacles that settled on dark panels grew to adult size no faster than those that settled on light panels.
choices.D: Larvae settled more densely on dark panels than on light ones at every depth at which the panels were hung.

explanation.why: Herrera explains the preference by how dark panels look; the text offers a rival explanation, the bacterial film that grows on dark panels. To weaken Herrera, a finding must show that the film, not the darkness, draws the larvae. If light panels carrying that film attract just as many larvae, darkness is not needed at all.
explanation.A: Incorrect. If larvae still prefer dark panels with no bacteria present, the film cannot explain the preference, so this supports Herrera.
explanation.B: Correct. When light panels with the film do as well as dark panels, the film alone accounts for the preference, which undercuts Herrera's visual explanation.
explanation.C: Incorrect. How fast barnacles grow after settling says nothing about why the larvae chose dark panels in the first place.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This only repeats the preference at more depths; it fits Herrera's explanation and the bacterial one equally well.
